title: Methane Uptake by Inland Waters: Fact or Fiction?
content:
Abstract

Inland waters are widely known as net emitters of methane (CH4) to the atmosphere, contributing ∼15% of global CH4 emissions. CH4 is produced by anaerobic methanogens in aquatic sediments, but net CH4 emissions at the water–air interface are modulated by CH4 oxidation by methanotrophs in the water column. However, the prevailing paradigm is that CH4 production outweighs oxidation, and that freshwaters are ubiquitously net emitters. Here, via data collation and solicitation of expert opinion, we show that diffusive CH4 uptake (i.e., net CH4 consumption) is reported across a diverse range of freshwater types, although fluxes are generally small (median = −2.2 mg CH4 m−2 d−1). Although some reports of freshwater CH4 uptake can be attributed to errors in data collection and analysis, others are harder to dismiss. Uptake is potentially driven by biological processes such as high rates of methanotrophy, or by physical processes such as mixing-induced introduction of low-CH4 water from other layers or inflows. Our results question the paradigm that freshwaters are always sources of CH4. We call for targeted field and lab work programs to more fully detect and understand this elusive but intriguing natural phenomenon.
